q: 1. The radius of gyration of a rectangular section is not proportional to
options: square root of the moment of inertia
square root of the inverse of the area
square root of the moment of inertia divided by area of the section
explain: k = √(I/A) — it depends jointly on I and A together, not on 1/A alone.

q: 2. The moment of inertia of a square section is given by
explain: For a square of side b, I = b⁴/12 (special case of bd³/12 with b=d).

q: 3. The moment of inertia of a rectangular (B×D) section about its base is
explain: About the base (not centroid), using parallel axis theorem: I_base = BD³/12 + BD(D/2)² = BD³/3.

q: 4. The moment of inertia of triangular section b×h about the base is
explain: Standard formula: I_base = bh³/12 for a triangle of base b and height h.

q: 5. The moment of inertia of triangular section b×h about the c.g. is
explain: Standard formula: I_cg = bh³/36 for a triangular section.

q: 6. Centre of gravity of a semi circle is ___ above the base AB (diameter)
explain: Standard result: centroid of a semicircular area lies at 4r/3π from the diameter.

q: 7. The c.g. of a semi-circular arc is
explain: As per the answer key for this set.

q: 8. Centrifugal force acts at a curve
explain: Centrifugal force is the outward pseudo-force acting away from the center of curvature.

q: 9. Centrifugal force is given by
explain: Centrifugal acceleration/specific force = v²/R (per unit mass form used in this option set).

q: 10. Centrifugal force acts away from the center of the path while centripetal force
options: acts away from the center of path
acts towards the centre of path
explain: As per the answer key for this set.

q: 11. A cable subjected to U.D.L. over its entire span assumes a shape of
explain: A cable under uniformly distributed load (per horizontal length) hangs in a parabolic shape.

q: 12. The algebraic sum of the shear flow of a section in any direction must be equal to
explain: Shear flow forms a self-balancing internal system, summing to zero around a closed section.

q: 13. The shear center may be defined as
options: the point through which the resultant of the shear stress passes
the point about which the moment of shear flow of section is zero
the shear force in that direction
explain: The shear center is the point of application of transverse load through which no twisting occurs — the resultant shear stress passes through it.

q: 14. The shear center in the case of a T-beam section is
options: at the C.G. of the section
at the neutral axis of the section
on the C.G. horizontal plane and away from C.G. within the leg projections
explain: For a T-section, the shear center coincides with the centroid due to its axis of symmetry.

q: 15. The maximum number of transverse shear forces possible at one end of an element of a plane frame are
explain: At each joint of a plane frame element, up to two transverse shear components can exist (in-plane, general loading).

q: 16. The maximum number of transverse shear forces possible at one end of an element of a plane truss are
explain: Truss members carry only axial force (two-force members) — no transverse shear develops at the ends.

q: 17. The law "Stress is proportional to strain within certain limits" is formulated by
explain: Hooke's Law states stress ∝ strain within the elastic limit.

q: 18. According to Hooke's law which one is correct?
explain: Hooke's Law: stress = Modulus of Elasticity × strain, i.e. σ = Eε.

q: 19. The zone between elastic limit and proportional limit on the elastic curve of an elastic material is known as
explain: Beyond the proportional limit but still within the elastic limit, stress-strain is no longer linear — this is the non-linear elastic zone.

q: 20. As per elastic theory of design the factor of safety is the ratio of
options: ultimate load to load at yield
explain: Factor of safety (elastic design) = yield stress / working (permissible) stress.

q: 21. Which of the following gives Poisson's ratio?
options: ratio of linear stress to linear strain
ratio of shear stress to shear strain
ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal strain
explain: Poisson's ratio μ = lateral strain / longitudinal strain.

q: 22. The value of Poisson's ratio always remains
explain: For all real engineering materials, Poisson's ratio lies between 0 and 0.5, always less than one.

q: 23. Normally the numerical value of Poisson's ratio is
explain: Typical values: steel ≈ 0.3, concrete ≈ 0.15.

q: 24. If the Poisson's ratio of a material is 0.25, the ratio of Modulus of Rigidity to the Young's Modulus is
25. The actual breaking stress of a ductile material from a tension test will be
options: less than the ultimate strength but greater than nominal breaking stress
explain: True (actual) stress is computed on the reduced necked area, so it exceeds the nominal ultimate strength (computed on original area).

q: 26. The phenomenon of decreased resistance of material due to reversal of stress is called
explain: Repeated/reversed stress cycles progressively weaken a material — this is fatigue.

q: 27. The property of a material by which a body returns to its original shape after removal of the force, is called
explain: Elasticity is the ability to recover original shape/size after unloading.

q: 28. A perfectly elastic body is
options: that body which recovers its original shape completely after removal of force
a body of such a material with a lot of extensibility
a body made of rubber only
a body whose cross sectional dimensions are very small
explain: By definition, perfect elasticity means complete shape recovery on unloading, regardless of material or size.

q: 29. The property of material by which it can be drawn, due to tension, to a smaller section, is called
explain: Ductility is the ability to be drawn into a wire/smaller section under tensile load.

q: 30. Which of the following is a relatively ductile material?
explain: Mild steel shows large plastic elongation before fracture, making it relatively ductile compared to the brittle options listed.

q: 31. The property of material by which it can be beaten or rolled into plates, is called
explain: Malleability is the ability to be hammered/rolled into thin sheets.

q: 32. A member which is subjected to reversible tensile or compressible stress may fail at a stress lower than the ultimate stress of the material. The property of metal, is called
explain: Failure under repeated/reversed stress below the ultimate stress is the fatigue phenomenon.

q: 33. The safe value of stress below which the material will not fail when subjected to reversal of stress is known as
explain: The endurance limit is the stress amplitude below which a material can withstand infinite stress reversals.

q: 34. The method of increasing fatigue resistance by over stressing the metal by successively increasing the loading is known as
explain: Coaxing improves fatigue strength by applying gradually increasing sub-critical stress cycles.

q: 35. The phenomenon of slow growth of strain under a steady tensile stress, i.e. increasing with time, is called
explain: Creep is time-dependent strain growth under sustained stress.

q: 36. If the value of Young's Modulus of elasticity for a material is zero, it implies that the material is
explain: Zero stiffness against elastic deformation implies the material deforms permanently/plastically under any stress.

q: 37. Limit of proportionality depends upon
explain: The proportional limit is a material property, varying with the type of material.

q: 38. The S.I. unit of modulus of elasticity is
explain: Modulus of elasticity has units of stress (force/area); the SI unit is N/m² (Pascal).

q: 39. Which of the following is dimensionless?
explain: Strain is a ratio of length change to original length — dimensionless.

q: 40. The stress at which extension of a material takes place more quickly as compared to the increase in load, is called
explain: At the yield point, strain increases disproportionately for a small increase in load.

q: 41. What is tenacity?
explain: Tenacity refers to the ultimate tensile strength of a material.

q: 42. Which of the following gives Modulus of Elasticity?
options: ratio of linear stress to linear strain
ratio of shear stress to shear strain
ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal strain
explain: Young's Modulus (E) = linear stress / linear strain.

q: 43. The Young's Modulus of elasticity is defined as a ratio of stress & strain within the
explain: Hooke's Law (and hence E) is valid only within the elastic limit.

q: 44. Which of the following gives Modulus of Rigidity?
options: ratio of linear stress to linear strain
ratio of shear stress to shear strain
ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal strain
explain: Modulus of Rigidity (N/G) = shear stress / shear strain.

q: 45. Which of the following gives Bulk Modulus?
options: ratio of linear stress to linear strain
ratio of shear stress to shear strain
ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal strain
ratio of the normal stress of equal magnitude on all six faces on a solid cube to the volumetric strain
explain: Bulk Modulus (K) = uniform normal stress / volumetric strain.

q: 46. Identify the correct relationship that exists among the modulus of elasticity (E), modulus of rigidity (N) and bulk modulus (k)
explain: Standard elastic-constants relation: E = 9KN / (3K + N).

q: 47. Normal strain is defined as
options: strain that is normal to shear strain
explain: Normal (linear) strain = change in length / original length.

q: 48. Shear strain is defined as
options: change in angle between planes at right angles
change in angles between two angles
explain: Shear strain is the change in the right angle between two originally perpendicular planes/lines.

q: 49. The modular ratio of two materials is defined as (E1 and E2 are the modulus of elasticity of the respective materials)
explain: Modular ratio m = E1/E2, used in composite-section analysis (e.g. RCC transformed sections).

q: 50. How does Young's Modulus vary with increase in temperature?
explain: Interatomic bonding weakens with rising temperature, reducing stiffness (E) for most materials.
